newsitem.title: USA: Authorities probe 429 church fire incidents.
newsitem.headline: Authorities probe 429 church fire incidents.

text.p: Authorities have investigated 429 incidents of arson, bombings and attempted bombings at churches -- mainly black houses of worship -- since January 1995, a government report issued on Sunday said.
A special task force created in June 1996 said in its first year's report that 199 persons were arrested. Federal, state and local prosecutors convicted 110 defendants involved in 77 fires.
"While we have made significant progress, the work of the task force is far from over," Assistant Treasury Secretary James Johnson told a news conference.
"Fires at houses of worship continue. Arrests continue to be made. And defendants continue to be prosecuted and convicted."

But Johson said the number of fires that ravaged churches frequented by both blacks and whites has "fallen dramatically" since President Clinton established the National Church Arson Task Force in June 1996.

The group coordinates the efforts of federal, state and local law enforcement. It includes officials from the Justice Department, the Treasury, the Department of Housing and Urban Development, and other agencies.
The task force's report said there was no evidence of a nationwide conspiracy and that motives ranged from racial hatred to vandalism to revenge.
This year investigators opened 82 investigations into arsons, bombings or attempted bombings. Nineteen involved predominately black churches and 63 involved other houses of worship.
In 1996 there were 298 incidents involving 117 black churches and 181 other houses of worship.
The task force said 160 of the 199 persons arrested were white, 34 black, and five Hispanic.
Eighty-three were juveniles. And of the 81 suspects arrested for arsons at black churches, 55 were white, 25 black, and one Hispanic.
"We have not seen hard evidence that would support the theory that there is a nationwide conspiracy," Johnson said.
"And we're seeing that many of the fires were committed by individuals acting alone."
